results.title: Over 50% of Text in EHR Notes is Duplicate Clinical Documentation | TechTarget
results.content: # Over 50% of Text in EHR Notes is Duplicate Clinical Documentation. ## Duplicate content in EHR notes increases the time for physicians to determine which data is accurate and creates viral copies of errors that can spread through clinical documentation. More than half of all text in EHR notes is duplicated, according to a study published in *JAMA Network Open* that suggests the need for a new clinical documentation paradigm that supports the stability of shared information over time. The duplicated half of the content provides no new data and increases the time required for the reading clinician to discern which information is accurate. “Instead, our study suggests that duplication is a rational response of clinicians attempting to manage information in a documentation paradigm ill-suited to the task,” they wrote. The prevalence of duplicate information suggests that a subset of clinical data remains true and relevant over time and should remain visible in the EHR.

results.content: (PDF) Hierarchical contrastive learning for multi-label text classification. Hierarchical contrastive learning for multi-label text classification. Multi-label text classification presents a significant challenge within the field of text classification, particularly due to the hierarchical nature of labels, where labels are organized in a tree-like structure that captures parent-child and sibling relationships. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a novel method called Hierarchical Contrastive Learning for Multi-label Text Classification (HCL-MTC). Specifically, we recast multi-label text classification as a multi-task learning problem, incorporating a hierarchical contrastive loss that is computed through a carefully designed sampling process. The overall structure of the HCL-MTC model (Hierarchical Contrastive Learning for Multi-label Text Classification), which elucidates the principal components and the process flow from input data to multi-label classification output. The model architecture is composed of a text encoder for capturing local and global textual features, a linear converter that transforms these features into label-specific representations, and a hierarchical contrastive learner which exploits the relationships between labels to enhance classification performance. The hierarchical contrastive learner is structured as a directed graph, where each node aggregates information from its parent, child, and self-nodes, guided by a learned weighted adjacency matrix that encodes label contrastive knowledge. Hierarchical multi-instance multi-label learning for Chinese patent text classification. To further enhance the accuracy of the Chinese patent classification, this paper proposes a model, based on the patent structure and takes the patent claim as subjects, with multi-instance multi-label learning as the main method. When formulated as a multi-label text classification (MTC) problem, it draws two challenges to existing models: one is to learn effective document representations from text content; the other is to model the cross-section behavior of label set. ### Modeling Text-Label Alignment for Hierarchical Text Classification. Building upon this framework, we introduce the Hierarchical Text-Label Alignment (HTLA) model, which leverages BERT as the text encoder and GPTrans as the graph encoder and integrates text-label embeddings to generate hierarchy-aware representations.

results.title: Severity of error in hierarchical datasets | Scientific Reports
results.content:
Title: Severity of error in hierarchical datasets | Scientific Reports
Various approaches to reduce severity for classification models are compared and evaluated in this work, which indicate that while many of them might be suited for a traditional image classification setting, there is a need for techniques tailored toward tasks and settings of medical domain to push artificial intelligence in healthcare to a deployable state. * The concept of Severity of Error (SoE) is introduced for the multi-label classification framework in the medical domain increasing its generalizability and adaption in various different use cases. * This work lays down the foundation for error severity of deep learning models in medical domain and opens up a new direction for future works. This work focuses on the medical domain and observes how introducing severity as a parameter changes the deep learning model performances in high-risk classification. These include tuning the dataset for severity, i.e. introducing a class taxonomy in it or balancing out the data samples and creating a cost matrix for the labels, which is termed a pre-training modification, while severity can also be injected into the training process and further it can also be used at inference time to reduce the cost of errors. Incorporating SoE in the training phase itself through the use of custom loss functions28 (2020).") such that any model can learn to choose the labels with the least severity. Figure 3 also indicates that while HXELoss reduces the severity of models, it is not able to train the models for a multilabel classification task properly and the models show low severity but also the low AUROC values. However, the proposed method would work for any data type, including time series data, for a classification-based task using a suitable deep learning model provided that the data is organized in some hierarchical structure. Further, the methods have been utilized for the standard classification task while a multi-label classification scenario has not been attempted while considering the severity of error or hierarchical datasets. The severity-reducing frameworks considered here are effective in reducing the severity in a multiclass classification setting however, they are not suitable for the multilabel datasets having *type-2* hierarchies that are common in the medical domain.

results.title: Developing New Methods Using Natural Language Processing to Label Text in Clinical Notes from Electronic Health Records | PCORI
results.content:
Title: Developing New Methods Using Natural Language Processing to Label Text in Clinical Notes from Electronic Health Records | PCORI
Clinical notes in electronic health records, or EHRs, may contain information that can help researchers study and compare treatments. Natural language processing, or NLP, methods can help researchers find and use information in EHR notes. In this study, the research team created and tested new NLP methods to automatically label text in EHR notes. Then, the research team created a new NLP labeling method called SILK-CA, which could automatically find and label text in EHR notes. Future research could test the NLP method with more EHR notes and more than one health topic. Researchers must manually extract information from clinical notes to create new NLP labels for each topic. ### Developing and Testing Software for Extracting COVID-19-Related Information from Clinical Notes in Electronic Health Records. Clinical notes in electronic health records, or EHRs, may contain information about COVID-19 that can help researchers study and compare treatments. Researchers can use computer programs based on natural language processing, or NLP, methods to find information in EHR notes. In this study, the research team created and tested a computer program based on NLP methods to find COVID-19 information in EHR clinical notes. The research team first created a guide about the types of COVID-19 information to label and extract from EHR notes. To develop and test NLP-based software to extract COVID-19-related information from EHR clinical notes. | Design | * Development of guidance for annotating EHR clinical notes with COVID-19-related information * Development of a reference data set of 400 clinical notes annotated with COVID-19 information * Software development |. First, the research team created annotation guidance that defined the COVID-19-related information to label and extract from EHR clinical notes. The health professionals labeled and extracted COVID-19-related information from one EHR clinical note from each patient in a random sample of 200 adult patients at two sites, Vanderbilt University Medical Center (VUMC) and Medical University of South Carolina (MUSC), for a total of 400 notes. Concurrently, the research team created and tested DECOVRI, an NLP-based software program, to extract COVID-19-related information from EHR notes. The research team used information from one EHR clinical note from each patient to create the reference data set and test the accuracy of the software.
